title: Jaap and the amrit bowl
hook: Jaap is one of the five banis recited over the iron bowl as amrit is prepared

segments.voice: Yesterday, sadaa, and your line, ever true, ever bliss: sadaa ang sange, ever by your side. Today, where else Jaap is heard, besides the morning.

A grandmother making soup. She doesn't just stir. She talks while she stirs: to the pot, to the kids in the doorway, sometimes under her breath to God. People who grew up in kitchens like that will swear the soup tasted different from anyone else's. Maybe it was the recipe. Maybe it was everything that got stirred in with it. In one Sikh ceremony, that idea is taken with complete seriousness: words are stirred into water for a long time, and Sikhs say the water is never the same again.

segments.voice: When a Sikh chooses to take amrit and join the Khalsa, the ceremony is called Amrit Sanchar. Five initiated Sikhs, the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, kneel around an iron bowl, a bata, filled with clean water. In go patashe, small sugar sweets. Then the water is stirred with a khanda, a double-edged sword, while the Panj Pyare recite five banis, one after another: first Japji, Guru Nanak's; second, Jaap Sahib; then the Tav Prasad Savaiye, Chaupai and Anand Sahib. Every stanza is recited over the water as it's stirred. So the salutations you've been learning, akaal, kripaal, aroop, ajooni, abhai, are recited into the water the new Khalsa drinks. The amrit is sprinkled on their eyes and hair, and they drink from the same bowl, whatever caste or family they came from. Tradition traces the ceremony to Vaisakhi in 1699, when the Tenth Guru first prepared amrit at Anandpur. A much-loved part of the story says the Guru's wife brought sugar sweets to the bowl, so that the iron and the steel would be joined by sweetness. Sources differ on the details, but Sikhs often say the point is clear: courage and kindness, stirred together. And the week ends here: the one-letter meter, abhai, fearlessness, the One in every land, death held in the One's hand, keeping the pace, the last stanza. And today, all of it, stirred in.
screen: `AMRIT SANCHAR: THE PANJ PYARE.` · `AN IRON BOWL, WATER, SUGAR, A KHANDA.` · `FIVE BANIS; JAAP IS THE SECOND.` · `SALUTATIONS STIRRED INTO WATER.` · then, large: `PRAYER STIRRED IN.`

segments.voice: This isn't amrit and isn't meant to copy the ceremony; it's only a way to feel what words stirred into water might mean. Fill a glass and stir it slowly, saying a line you know, namastvam akaale, namastvam kripaale, then set the spoon down and drink the water slowly.
Amrit. The nectar of immortality — the water stirred in the iron bowl while Jaap, the second of five banis, is recited over it for the Khalsa.
Your line: prayer stirred in. Courage and kindness, stirred together in one bowl. A week, done.

chat.says: What does Jaap Sahib have to do with becoming a Khalsa Sikh?
options: It's the second of five banis recited over the amrit as it's stirred in the iron bowl.
Nothing; Jaap is only said alone in the morning, never in the ceremony.
It's the first prayer read, before any other, and the only one recited.
